strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: semantic segmentation without user-supplied class names. Generating an image-specific vocabulary and passing it to an existing segmentor offers a practical route to automating open-vocabulary segmentation without additional neural-network fine-tuning.

Decoding subsets of clustered BLIP patch embeddings is an interesting technical contribution. Reusing BLIP for both feature extraction and regional captioning provides a relatively simple way to discover objects missed by global captions.

Table 1 provides encouraging evidence across three datasets: Self-Seg improves class-agnostic mIoU over BLIP plus X-Decoder from 38.0 to 41.9 on VOC, 26.7 to 29.2 on ADE20K, and 29.2 to 35.8 on Cityscapes. Table 3 also demonstrates the benefit of repeated captioning for complex scenes.

The pipeline is explained with helpful diagrams, implementation parameters, and evaluator pseudocode. Appendix B usefully documents hallucinated labels, competing category names, and overly generic descriptions, alongside successful examples.
weaknesses: The proposed LOVE evaluator directly determines Self-Seg's semantic scores but is not validated against human judgments or alternative mappings. Appendix A instructs the LLM to map stuff descriptions to background, although ADE20K and Cityscapes annotate stuff categories; exact-name overrides only partly mitigate this problem. For ADE20K, the prompt relies on the LLM remembering the dataset vocabulary rather than supplying its 847 classes. Mapping accuracy, coverage, and sensitivity are unreported, leaving the main quantitative evidence uncertain.

The headline comparison with ZeroSeg—41.6 versus 20.1 mIoU on VOC—is not established under a common label-mapping protocol. Section 3.4 describes different evaluators, but no controlled reevaluation is reported. The comparison also needs explicit accounting for the segmentation supervision inherited through pretrained X-Decoder. No automatic-class competitor is evaluated on ADE20K or Cityscapes, limiting the support for the state-of-the-art claims.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the main contribution. The plain-caption baseline is evaluated only with class-agnostic mIoU, which ignores class-name correctness and has no explicit penalty for unmatched predictions. Semantic mIoU and vocabulary precision/recall would better test category discovery. Controls for caption budget and ablations of multiscale clustering, alignment, and denoising are needed to establish which components produce the gains.

Model selection and statistical reliability are insufficiently documented. Section 4.1 reports Bayesian hyperparameter optimization on VOC without identifying a separate tuning split, while Table 2 uses the dataset-specific best caption counts from Table 3. Disjoint tuning and evaluation data are not established, and stochastic caption generation is evaluated without variation across repeated runs.

Several implementation details impede reproduction: Equation 10 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the stated Hungarian matching; cross-resolution alignment is underspecified; and the treatment of concatenated 256-dimensional positional features before the frozen BLIP decoder is unclear. Runtime and memory measurements are also missing despite repeated regional captioning. These concerns are secondary to the evaluation issues but require clarification.
